messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ayesha was a 31-year-old South Asian woman who had been teaching elementary school for eight years when the accident happened, and the ordinary confidence she had brought into her classroom changed in a single afternoon. She had been driving home after school with her husband when she misjudged a turn and, in the confusion, struck a cyclist in the crosswalk. The man survived, but he was badly injured, and Ayesha has never been able to let herself call it “an accident” in the casual way other people did. In the days afterward, she found that the memory did not sit in the past at all. It arrived as a sequence of frozen pictures: the light at the intersection, the bicycle tipping, the man on the pavement, her own hands locked on the wheel. When she tried to speak about it, she could sometimes smell the sharp, bitter scent of hot rubber and dust from the road, and that smell seemed to pull her straight back into the scene, as if the afternoon were still unfolding around her.

What frightened Ayesha most was how complete the moment felt when it returned. The event did not come back as a story she could tell herself had ended; it came back with the force of happening now, and the more she was reminded of it, the more immediate it became. Hearing a colleague mention a car crash in the staff room or seeing news about accidents would make her chest tighten and her mind snap back to that intersection. Even something as simple as being praised for her teaching — a parent thanking her for the way she handled a child, or the principal complimenting her lesson plans — could unsettle her. She would feel the positive attention and, instead of comfort, a strange confusion and dread, because any moment that made her feel proud or seen seemed to threaten the memory’s return. In those moments, she would suddenly be back in the car in her mind, replaying the impact as though she were still trapped inside it.

Ayesha had come to believe that the accident happened because of the way she acted, that her own lapse had caused another person’s suffering, and from that she drew a harsher conclusion about herself. She no longer felt capable of doing the things that had once defined her — being calm, competent, and reliable — and she began to see herself as permanently changed, a person who did not belong among others in the same way anymore. That sense of being an outsider colored the rest of her life. At school, she kept to herself in the staff room and let conversations drift past if they turned toward driving, roads, or anything that might turn into talk about accidents. She noticed that even when the discussion was only casual, her body reacted before she could think: her mind would flash to the crash, and the old images would crowd in again. Because the memory felt so vivid and alive, any mention of accidents seemed to open the door to it, and once it was open she became more convinced that she was dangerous, damaged, and fundamentally different from the other teachers around her.

Over the following months, Ayesha started arranging her days around the hope of never being caught by those moments of praise, joy, or accident talk. She worked harder to avoid situations where she might be singled out for good performance, even though teaching had once been a source of pride. At home, she grew quiet when her husband tried to reassure her that anyone could make a mistake, because hearing that only sharpened her self-blame. The more she judged herself as no longer capable, the more quickly she scanned for signs that something might remind her of the crash, and the more readily those reminders brought the whole scene back in vivid snapshots. She came to therapy after realizing that she was beginning to withdraw not only from colleagues but from the version of herself she had once known, and she was afraid that if she kept living this way she would lose her classroom, her marriage’s ease, and the last thread of confidence she had left. What finally brought her in was the fear that she would remain forever stuck in that intersection, hoping instead that treatment might help her understand why the memory keeps returning with such force and whether she can ever feel like a capable person again.
